chapter: Ch 8 — Declaration and Payment of Dividend

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 2(35) · Meaning of dividend
questions.stem: Section 2(35) of the Companies Act 2013 defines "dividend" by providing that it:

readLink.label: Read: Meaning of dividend — final and interim →

options.text: means the share of divisible profits distributed to members, computed after providing for depreciation under Schedule II
options.explanation: That is a description of what a dividend commercially is, and it borrows the depreciation requirement from s. 123(2). Section 2(35) itself does not define dividend in those terms.

options.text: means any distribution made by a company to its members, whether out of profits or out of capital
options.explanation: A distribution out of capital is precisely what s. 123 forbids. No definition in the Act permits it.

options.text: includes any interim dividend
options.explanation: Correct. Section 2(35) is an inclusive definition of one line, and its whole effect is to bring interim dividend within every provision that speaks of "dividend" — the five-day deposit, the thirty-day payment clock and s. 127.

options.text: excludes any interim dividend, which is governed separately by section 123(3)
options.explanation: The opposite of the truth. Section 123(3) supplies the source and rate rules for interim dividend, but s. 2(35) makes the general dividend machinery apply to it as well.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · Declaration of final dividend
questions.stem: A final dividend for a financial year is declared by:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 123 read with Table F, Schedule I

readLink.label: Read: Meaning of dividend — final and interim →

options.text: the Board of Directors, at a meeting of the Board held before the annual general meeting
options.explanation: The Board recommends a final dividend; it declares only an interim dividend under s. 123(3).

options.text: the members in general meeting, on the recommendation of the Board of Directors
options.explanation: Correct. The Board recommends and the members declare. Without a Board recommendation the members have nothing to declare.

options.text: the members in general meeting, whether or not the Board has recommended a dividend
options.explanation: The recommendation is the foundation of the members' power. Members cannot originate a final dividend on their own motion.

options.text: the Board of Directors, subject to ratification by the members at the next annual general meeting
options.explanation: Ratification has no role here. The declaration itself is the members' act, and it creates the debt.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · Rate recommended by the Board
questions.stem: The Board of Anaya Ceramics Limited recommends a final dividend of 14 per cent. At the annual general meeting the members resolve to declare 18 per cent, pointing to the size of the company's free reserves. The resolution is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 123 read with Table F, Regulation 80

readLink.label: Read: Meaning of dividend — final and interim →

options.text: valid, because the members are the owners of the reserves and the general meeting is supreme
options.explanation: Supremacy of the general meeting does not survive an express restriction. The members may not exceed the recommended rate.

options.text: valid, provided the increased dividend still satisfies section 123(1) as to source
options.explanation: Satisfying the source test is necessary but not sufficient. The rate ceiling is a separate and independent restriction.

options.text: valid to the extent of 14 per cent and void as to the excess, so 18 per cent stands reduced automatically
options.explanation: Attractive but wrong in form. The resolution as passed is one the company cannot act on; the members must instead declare a rate not exceeding the recommendation.

options.text: not one the company may act on, because the members may reduce or refuse the recommended dividend but may never exceed it
options.explanation: Correct. The rate ceiling is one-directional: the members may declare 14 per cent, any lower figure, or nothing at all, but never more than the Board recommended.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 123(3) · Who declares an interim dividend
questions.stem: Under section 123(3), an interim dividend may be declared by:

readLink.label: Read: Interim dividend and its rate cap →

options.text: the Board of Directors, during any financial year or at any time from the closure of the financial year till the holding of the annual general meeting
options.explanation: Correct. Section 123(3) names the Board as the declaring authority and fixes both limbs of the window in exactly these words.

options.text: the members in general meeting, on the recommendation of the Board
options.explanation: That is the route for a final dividend. An interim dividend needs no general meeting at all.

options.text: the Board of Directors, but only during the financial year and never after it has closed
options.explanation: This drops the second limb of the window. The Board may declare an interim dividend after the year closes, so long as the annual general meeting has not yet been held.

options.text: the Board of Directors, with the previous approval of the Registrar of Companies
options.explanation: No approval of the Registrar is required for any dividend under the Act.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 123(1)(a) · Sources of dividend
questions.stem: Under section 123(1)(a), dividend for a financial year may be declared out of:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 123(1)(a) read with s. 123(2)

readLink.label: Read: Sources of dividend — section 123 →

options.text: the profits of the company for that financial year only, computed before providing for depreciation
options.explanation: Two errors: depreciation under Schedule II must be provided for, and previous years' undistributed profits are an equally valid source.

options.text: the securities premium account and the capital redemption reserve, both being reserves of the company
options.explanation: Neither is a free reserve, and the fourth proviso to s. 123(1) forbids dividend out of reserves other than free reserves.

options.text: the profits of the company for that year after providing for depreciation, or the undistributed profits of any previous financial year or years after providing for depreciation, or out of both
options.explanation: Correct. Section 123(1)(a) offers three permutations — the current year, earlier years, or both — and attaches the Schedule II depreciation condition to each.

options.text: any reserve of the company, provided the Board records in its minutes that the distribution is prudent
options.explanation: A Board minute cannot override a statutory prohibition. Only free reserves qualify.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 123(1)(b) · Government-guaranteed dividend
questions.stem: Apart from profits, section 123(1) permits a dividend to be declared out of:

readLink.label: Read: Sources of dividend — section 123 →

options.text: the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made during the financial year
options.explanation: Issue proceeds are share capital. Paying dividend out of them is a return of capital, which the section exists to prevent.

options.text: money provided by the Central Government or a State Government for the payment of dividend, in pursuance of a guarantee given by that Government
options.explanation: Correct. Section 123(1)(b) is the one source in the chapter that has nothing to do with profits, and it is examined because students overlook it.

options.text: money borrowed from a scheduled bank against the security of the company's receivables
options.explanation: Borrowed money is not a source of dividend under any limb of s. 123(1).

options.text: the revaluation surplus arising on a professional valuation of the company's immovable property
options.explanation: Section 2(43) expressly excludes unrealised gains and revaluation of assets from free reserves, so a revaluation surplus can never fund a dividend.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 123(1) fourth proviso · Free reserves only
questions.stem: Nandan Alloys Limited proposes to declare dividend out of its debenture redemption reserve, its securities premium account and its free reserves. Which of these may lawfully be used?

readLink.label: Read: Sources of dividend — section 123 →

options.text: All three, since each is a reserve appearing in the audited balance sheet
options.explanation: Appearing in the balance sheet is not the test. The proviso restricts the source to free reserves.

options.text: The debenture redemption reserve and the free reserves, but not the securities premium account
options.explanation: A debenture redemption reserve is an appropriation set aside for a specific statutory purpose and is not available for distribution as dividend.

options.text: The securities premium account and the free reserves, because securities premium represents realised money
options.explanation: Realisation is irrelevant. The securities premium account may be applied only for the purposes the Act specifies, and dividend is not among them.

options.text: Only the free reserves, because no dividend may be declared or paid from reserves other than free reserves
options.explanation: Correct. The fourth proviso to s. 123(1) confines the source to free reserves as defined in s. 2(43).

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 2(43) · Free reserves
questions.stem: Which of the following is excluded from "free reserves" by section 2(43)?

readLink.label: Read: Sources of dividend — section 123 →

options.text: Any amount representing unrealised gains, notional gains or revaluation of assets, whether shown as a reserve or otherwise
options.explanation: Correct. Section 2(43) excludes unrealised and notional gains and revaluation amounts, and also any change in the carrying amount of an asset or liability recognised in equity on fair-value measurement.

options.text: The undistributed profits of previous financial years that have been transferred to the general reserve
options.explanation: These are the classic free reserves. They are exactly what Rule 3 contemplates a company drawing on.

options.text: Any reserve created out of profits by a voluntary transfer under the first proviso to section 123(1)
options.explanation: A voluntary transfer out of profits remains available for distribution and stays within free reserves.

options.text: The surplus standing to the credit of the profit and loss account
options.explanation: The surplus in the profit and loss account is available for distribution and is not excluded; s. 123(3) even names it as a source for interim dividend.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 123(1) first proviso · Transfer to reserves
questions.stem: Before declaring dividend for a financial year, a company under the Companies Act 2013:

readLink.label: Read: Sources of dividend — section 123 →

options.text: must transfer at least ten per cent of its profits for that year to reserves
options.explanation: A slab of compulsory transfer existed under the Companies Act 1956. The 2013 Act abolished it, and named percentages in the options are testing exactly that memory.

options.text: must transfer such percentage of its profits to reserves as the Central Government may prescribe for its class of company
options.explanation: No such prescription operates. The first proviso leaves the percentage to the company's own judgment.

options.text: may transfer such percentage of its profits for that year to its reserves as it considers appropriate
options.explanation: Correct. The first proviso to s. 123(1) makes the transfer wholly voluntary, and leaves the percentage to the company.

options.text: is forbidden to transfer any part of the year's profits to reserves until the dividend has been paid
options.explanation: The proviso contemplates the transfer being made before the declaration, not after payment.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 123(1) third proviso · Set-off of past losses
questions.stem: Ojaswi Foods Limited earns a profit of ₹60,00,000 for the year after Schedule II depreciation. It carries forward a loss of ₹18,00,000 and depreciation of ₹7,00,000 that was not provided for in earlier years. Before declaring any dividend the company must:

readLink.label: Read: Sources of dividend — section 123 →

options.text: set off the carried-over loss of ₹18,00,000 only, unprovided depreciation of earlier years being a matter for the auditors
options.explanation: The third proviso names both — carried-over losses AND depreciation not provided in previous year or years.

options.text: set off both the carried-over loss of ₹18,00,000 and the unprovided depreciation of ₹7,00,000 against the current year's profit, leaving ₹35,00,000
options.explanation: Correct. The third proviso to s. 123(1) requires both to be set off against the profit of the current year, so ₹60,00,000 − ₹18,00,000 − ₹7,00,000 = ₹35,00,000 is the distributable figure.

options.text: set off nothing, since the profit for the current year has already been arrived at after providing depreciation for that year
options.explanation: The current year's depreciation is a s. 123(2) requirement. The third proviso deals separately with earlier years' shortfalls and earlier years' losses.

options.text: transfer ₹25,00,000 to a special reserve and declare dividend out of the balance
options.explanation: There is no such special-reserve mechanism. The proviso requires a set-off against current profit, not an appropriation.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · Rule 3(1) · Average of the three preceding rates
questions.stem: Bhavani Ceramics Limited has inadequate profits for the year to 31 March 2026 and proposes to declare dividend out of accumulated profits transferred to its free reserves. It declared dividend at 12 per cent, 9 per cent and 6 per cent in the three immediately preceding financial years. The maximum rate at which it may declare dividend, applying the first condition of Rule 3, is:
questions.sourceRef: Rule 3(1), Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014

readLink.label: Read: Dividend out of accumulated profits — Rule 3 →

options.text: 9 per cent
options.explanation: Correct. The condition caps the rate at the average of the three immediately preceding years' rates: (12 + 9 + 6) ÷ 3 = 9 per cent.

options.text: 12 per cent
options.explanation: That is the highest of the three rates. Rule 3 prescribes the average, not the highest.

options.text: 6 per cent
options.explanation: That is the lowest of the three rates. The rule takes the average, not the most conservative figure.

options.text: 27 per cent
options.explanation: That is the sum of the three rates. The averaging step has been omitted.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · Rule 3(2) · The one-tenth draw ceiling
questions.stem: Chandrika Polymers Limited's latest audited financial statement shows a paid-up share capital of ₹6,00,00,000 and free reserves of ₹4,00,00,000. Its profits for the year are inadequate and it proposes to draw on accumulated profits. The maximum total amount it may draw, applying the second condition of Rule 3, is:
questions.sourceRef: Rule 3(2), Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014

readLink.label: Read: Dividend out of accumulated profits — Rule 3 →

options.explanation: That is one-tenth of the paid-up share capital alone. The condition is measured on capital PLUS free reserves.
That is one-tenth of the free reserves alone, again dropping half of the base.
That is fifteen per cent of the paid-up share capital — the base for the third condition, which is a floor on what must be left behind, not a ceiling on what may be drawn.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · Rule 3(4) · The fifteen-per-cent reserve floor
questions.stem: Dhanashree Mills Limited's latest audited financial statement shows a paid-up share capital of ₹20,00,00,000 and free reserves of ₹4,00,00,000. Ignoring the rate ceiling, the maximum amount it may draw from its accumulated profits is:
questions.sourceRef: Rule 3(2) and 3(4), Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014

readLink.label: Read: Dividend out of accumulated profits — Rule 3 →

options.explanation: That applies only the one-tenth condition — one-tenth of ₹24,00,00,000. Drawing that much would leave reserves of ₹1,60,00,000, below the fifteen-per-cent floor of ₹3,00,00,000.

Correct. The floor requires reserves after the withdrawal to be at least 15% × ₹20,00,00,000 = ₹3,00,00,000, so at most ₹4,00,00,000 − ₹3,00,00,000 = ₹1,00,00,000 may be drawn. Here the floor bites before the one-tenth cap does.
That is the whole of the free reserves. Both the one-tenth ceiling and the fifteen-per-cent floor forbid it.
That is the fifteen-per-cent floor itself — the amount that must REMAIN, not the amount that may be taken.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · Rule 3 · Maximum dividend on all three conditions
questions.stem: Ekaanta Instruments Limited has a paid-up equity share capital of ₹9,00,00,000 and free reserves of ₹5,00,00,000 per its latest audited financial statement. It has incurred a loss of ₹40,00,000 for the current financial year. Dividend rates in the three immediately preceding years were 14 per cent, 11 per cent and 8 per cent. The maximum dividend it may declare out of accumulated profits is:
questions.sourceRef: Rule 3, Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014

readLink.label: Read: Dividend out of accumulated profits — Rule 3 →

options.explanation: That is only the one-tenth draw ceiling. It ignores both the set-off of the current year's loss out of the draw and the independent rate ceiling.
That is the draw ceiling of ₹1,40,00,000 less the ₹40,00,000 loss set-off — correct as far as it goes, but the rate ceiling of 11 per cent on ₹9,00,00,000 caps the dividend lower still.

Correct. The rate ceiling is the average of 14, 11 and 8 = 11 per cent; 11% × ₹9,00,00,000 = ₹99,00,000. The total draw of ₹99,00,000 + ₹40,00,000 = ₹1,39,00,000 is within the ₹1,40,00,000 one-tenth cap, and the reserves left, ₹3,61,00,000, exceed the ₹1,35,00,000 floor.
That applies 14 per cent — the highest of the three preceding rates — instead of their average.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 123(3) proviso · Interim rate cap after a loss
questions.stem: Falguni Textiles Limited has a paid-up equity share capital of ₹3,00,00,000. It has incurred a loss for the year 2026-27 up to the end of the quarter ended 31 December 2026, although the surplus in its profit and loss account stands at ₹1,10,00,000. On 20 January 2027 the Board proposes an interim dividend. Dividend rates for the three immediately preceding financial years were 18, 15 and 9 per cent. The maximum interim dividend the Board may declare is:

readLink.label: Read: Interim dividend and its rate cap →

options.explanation: Correct. The proviso to s. 123(3) caps the rate at the average of the three preceding years — (18 + 15 + 9) ÷ 3 = 14 per cent — so 14% × ₹3,00,00,000 = ₹42,00,000. The source remains the surplus in the profit and loss account, which s. 123(3) expressly allows.
That is 18 per cent, the highest of the three rates. The proviso prescribes the average.
That is one-tenth of the paid-up capital, importing the Rule 3 draw ceiling into an interim dividend. Rule 3 has no application to s. 123(3).
That is 9 per cent, the lowest of the three rates. The proviso takes the average, not the least favourable figure.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · Rule 3(1) proviso · The exception to the rate ceiling
questions.stem: The condition capping the rate of dividend at the average of the three immediately preceding years' rates does not apply to a company which:
questions.sourceRef: Proviso to Rule 3(1), Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014

readLink.label: Read: Dividend out of accumulated profits — Rule 3 →

options.text: has declared dividend in only one of the three immediately preceding financial years
options.explanation: The exception requires no dividend in EACH of the three preceding years. A company that paid in one of them is still inside the condition.

options.text: has adequate profits in the current financial year
options.explanation: A company with adequate profits does not need Rule 3 at all; it declares out of current profits under s. 123(1)(a). The exception is not about that situation.

options.text: has transferred more than ten per cent of its profits to reserves in each of the three preceding years
options.explanation: The size of past transfers to reserves is irrelevant to the rate ceiling.

options.text: has not declared any dividend in each of the three immediately preceding financial years
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso to the first condition lifts the rate ceiling only where the company declared no dividend in each of those three years, there being no average to work from. The one-tenth ceiling and the fifteen-per-cent floor continue to apply.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · Rule 3(3) · Set-off of the current year's loss
questions.stem: Where a company draws on accumulated profits under Rule 3 and has also incurred a loss in the financial year in which the dividend is declared, the amount drawn:
questions.sourceRef: Rule 3(3), Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014

readLink.label: Read: Dividend out of accumulated profits — Rule 3 →

options.text: may be applied wholly to the dividend, the current year's loss being carried forward for set-off in a later year
options.explanation: That reverses the rule. The loss must be absorbed out of the draw before any equity dividend is declared.

options.text: shall first be used to set off the losses incurred in that financial year, before any dividend in respect of equity shares is declared
options.explanation: Correct. This is the third condition of Rule 3, and it reduces the amount of the draw available for distribution rupee for rupee.

options.text: shall be reduced by fifteen per cent of the current year's loss
options.explanation: There is no proportionate reduction anywhere in Rule 3. The whole loss is set off, and fifteen per cent belongs to the reserve floor.

options.text: is unaffected, because Rule 3 applies only where there is an absence of profits and not where there is a loss
options.explanation: Rule 3 applies on inadequacy OR absence of profits, and a loss is the clearest case of absence. The third condition is drafted precisely for it.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 123(6) · Deposit defaults bar dividend
questions.stem: Gargi Infratech Limited has failed to repay a matured public deposit and the failure continues. Its profits for the year are ample. As regards dividend on its equity shares, the company:

readLink.label: Read: Sources of dividend — section 123 →

options.text: may declare dividend, since sections 73 and 74 concern depositors and not members
options.explanation: Section 123(6) expressly links the two. The depositor's protection is enforced by suspending the members' dividend.

options.text: may declare dividend with the previous approval of the Tribunal
options.explanation: The bar is automatic and admits of no dispensation by the Tribunal or anyone else.

options.text: shall not declare any dividend on its equity shares so long as the failure continues
options.explanation: Correct. Section 123(6) suspends the power automatically while an ss. 73/74 failure subsists, whatever the state of the profits, and the power revives when the default is cured.

options.text: is permanently disqualified from declaring dividend on its equity shares
options.explanation: The bar lasts only "so long as such failure continues". Curing the default restores the power.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 123(3) · Sources for an interim dividend
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a source out of which section 123(3) permits an interim dividend to be declared?

readLink.label: Read: Interim dividend and its rate cap →

options.text: The securities premium account of the company
options.explanation: Correct as the answer to a NOT question. Section 123(3) names the surplus in the profit and loss account, the profits of the financial year concerned, and the profits generated till the quarter preceding declaration. The securities premium account is not a free reserve and appears nowhere in the sub-section.

options.text: The surplus in the profit and loss account
options.explanation: Expressly named in s. 123(3), and often the only pool available where the year so far has been unprofitable.

options.text: The profits of the financial year for which the interim dividend is sought to be declared
options.explanation: Expressly named in s. 123(3).

options.text: The profits generated in the financial year till the quarter preceding the date of declaration of the interim dividend
options.explanation: Expressly named in s. 123(3), and it is the same quarter that the loss proviso then measures.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 123(3) · The interim declaration window
questions.stem: The period during which the Board may declare an interim dividend runs:

readLink.label: Read: Interim dividend and its rate cap →

options.text: only from the first day of the financial year to the last day of that financial year
options.explanation: This drops the second limb. The Board may also act after the year has closed, until the annual general meeting is held.

options.text: only from the closure of the financial year till the holding of the annual general meeting
options.explanation: This drops the first limb. An interim dividend may of course be declared during the year itself — that is its ordinary use.

options.text: from the closure of the financial year till the filing of the annual return with the Registrar
options.explanation: The window closes at the annual general meeting, not at the filing of the annual return.

options.text: during any financial year, and also at any time during the period from the closure of the financial year till the holding of the annual general meeting
options.explanation: Correct. Section 123(3) contains both limbs, and the second was inserted precisely to cover the gap between the year-end and the annual general meeting.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 123(4) · The five-day deposit clock
questions.stem: The members of Suryodaya Ceramics Limited declare a final dividend at the annual general meeting held on 12 August 2026. The last date by which the amount of the dividend must be deposited in a separate account with a scheduled bank is:

readLink.label: Read: Depositing and paying the dividend →

options.text: 16 August 2026
options.explanation: That counts the day of declaration itself as day one. The five days run from the date of declaration, so the last date is 17 August 2026.

options.text: 17 August 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Section 123(4) allows five days from the date of declaration; 12 August plus five days is 17 August 2026.

options.text: 19 August 2026
options.explanation: That is seven days. Seven days is the s. 124(1) transfer period, and it runs from the expiry of the thirty-day payment period, not from declaration.

options.text: 11 September 2026
options.explanation: That is thirty days from declaration — the s. 127 payment deadline, not the deposit deadline.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 123(4) · Where the dividend must be deposited
questions.stem: Section 123(4) requires the amount of the dividend to be deposited:

readLink.label: Read: Depositing and paying the dividend →

options.text: in the company's existing current account with any bank, earmarked in its books as dividend payable
options.explanation: An earmarking entry is not enough. The sub-section requires a separate account, so that the money is physically segregated.

options.text: in a separate account with any bank, co-operative or scheduled, within thirty days of declaration
options.explanation: Two errors: the bank must be a SCHEDULED bank, and the period is five days, not thirty.

options.text: in a separate account with a scheduled bank, within five days of the date of declaration, and this applies to interim dividend as well
options.explanation: Correct. Section 123(4) names the separate account, the scheduled bank and the five-day period, and expressly extends the obligation to interim dividend.

options.text: in the Unpaid Dividend Account maintained under section 124
options.explanation: The Unpaid Dividend Account receives only what remains unpaid or unclaimed after the thirty days, and it is a later and different account.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 127 · The thirty-day payment clock
questions.stem: Haritha Agro Limited declares a final dividend at its annual general meeting held on 24 August 2026. The last date by which the dividend must be paid, or the warrant in respect of it posted, is:

readLink.label: Read: Depositing and paying the dividend →

options.text: 23 September 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Section 127 allows thirty days from the date of declaration; 24 August plus thirty days is 23 September 2026.

options.text: 24 September 2026
options.explanation: That treats the period as one calendar month. Section 127 speaks of thirty days, and August has thirty-one.

options.text: 29 August 2026
options.explanation: That is the five-day deposit deadline under s. 123(4), a different obligation from the same starting date.

options.text: 30 September 2026
options.explanation: That is the last date for transferring the unpaid balance to the Unpaid Dividend Account — seven days after the thirty-day period expires.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 123(5) · To whom dividend is payable
questions.stem: Under section 123(5), dividend in respect of a share may be paid to:

readLink.label: Read: Depositing and paying the dividend →

options.text: the registered shareholder only, and to no one else in any circumstances
options.explanation: Too narrow. The sub-section also permits payment to his order and to his banker.

options.text: any person in whose favour the shareholder has executed an instrument of transfer, whether or not it has been registered
options.explanation: An unregistered transferee has no claim under s. 123(5). Section 126 sends the dividend on such shares into the Unpaid Dividend Account instead.

options.text: the beneficial owner identified by the company, irrespective of the register of members
options.explanation: The sub-section keys payment to the REGISTERED holder. It does not authorise the company to look behind the register.

options.text: the registered shareholder, or to his order, or to his banker
options.explanation: Correct. Those three are the only permitted payees, and payment must be in cash — which may be made by cheque, warrant or electronic mode.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 123(5) provisos · Dividend in kind and bonus shares
questions.stem: Indrayani Motors Limited proposes to satisfy its declared dividend by distributing shares it holds in a subsidiary, and separately proposes a bonus issue of fully paid-up shares out of free reserves. Which statement is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 123(5) and its provisos

readLink.label: Read: Depositing and paying the dividend →

options.text: Both are permissible, since a distribution of shares is a distribution of value and the shareholders consent
options.explanation: Consent cannot cure the statutory bar. Dividend shall not be payable except in cash.

options.text: The distribution of the subsidiary's shares as dividend is not permissible, but the bonus issue is, being a capitalisation of profits or reserves saved by the first proviso
options.explanation: Correct. Section 123(5) bars dividend otherwise than in cash, so a dividend in kind is out; the first proviso expressly preserves the capitalisation of profits or reserves for a fully paid bonus issue, and no cash leaves the company.

options.text: Neither is permissible, because both distribute assets of the company otherwise than in cash
options.explanation: The first proviso to s. 123(5) exists precisely to save the bonus issue, and also the paying up of amounts unpaid on members' shares.

options.text: Both are permissible only if the articles of the company expressly authorise payment of dividend in kind
options.explanation: No article can authorise what the section forbids. Section 51 is the only place in this chapter where an enabling article matters.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 124(1) · The seven-day transfer clock
questions.stem: Ganga Foods Limited declares a final dividend on 6 November 2026. At the end of the period allowed for payment, ₹4,50,000 remains unpaid and unclaimed. The last date by which that amount must be transferred to the Unpaid Dividend Account is:

readLink.label: Read: Unpaid dividend and the Unpaid Dividend Account — section 124 →

options.text: 13 November 2026
options.explanation: That counts the seven days from the date of declaration. Section 124(1) counts them from the EXPIRY of the thirty-day payment period.

options.text: 6 December 2026
options.explanation: That is the expiry of the thirty-day payment period itself. The seven-day transfer period begins there and has not yet run.

options.text: 13 December 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Thirty days from 6 November 2026 expire on 6 December 2026; seven days from that expiry gives 13 December 2026.

options.text: 5 January 2027
options.explanation: That is a further thirty days after the payment period. Section 124(1) allows seven days, not thirty.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 124(2) · The ninety-day statement
questions.stem: After transferring unpaid dividend to the Unpaid Dividend Account, a company must, within ninety days of making that transfer:

readLink.label: Read: Unpaid dividend and the Unpaid Dividend Account — section 124 →

options.text: prepare a statement of the names, last known addresses and unpaid dividend of each person entitled, and place it on its own website, if any, and on any other website approved by the Central Government
options.explanation: Correct. Section 124(2) requires the statement within ninety days of the transfer, and requires both placements — the company's own website where it has one, and the approved website.

options.text: file the statement with the Registrar of Companies and publish it in two newspapers
options.explanation: Newspaper publication belongs to s. 13(8), on a change of objects with unspent prospectus money. Section 124(2) requires website placement.

options.text: transfer the amount to the Investor Education and Protection Fund
options.explanation: That transfer comes only after seven years from the date of the transfer into the Unpaid Dividend Account.

options.text: send individual notices by registered post to every shareholder whose dividend remains unclaimed
options.explanation: Individual registered-post notices are not what the sub-section prescribes; a published statement is.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 124(3) · Twelve per cent and who benefits
questions.stem: Where a company defaults in transferring unpaid dividend to the Unpaid Dividend Account, section 124(3) provides that:

readLink.label: Read: Unpaid dividend and the Unpaid Dividend Account — section 124 →

options.text: the company shall pay interest at eighteen per cent per annum from the date of the default, which is retained by the company as a provision
options.explanation: Both halves are wrong. Eighteen per cent is the s. 127 rate for failing to pay the dividend, and the interest under s. 124(3) does not stay with the company.

options.text: the company shall pay interest at twelve per cent per annum from the date of declaration of the dividend
options.explanation: The rate is right but the starting point is wrong: interest runs from the date of the DEFAULT in transferring, not from the declaration.

options.text: the Tribunal may impose interest at such rate as it thinks fit on an application by any member
options.explanation: No application to the Tribunal is needed. The obligation is automatic and the rate is fixed by the sub-section.

options.text: the company shall pay interest at twelve per cent per annum from the date of the default on so much of the amount as has not been transferred, and that interest enures to the benefit of the members in proportion to the amounts remaining unpaid to them
options.explanation: Correct. Section 124(3) fixes twelve per cent, runs it from the date of the default, applies it only to the untransferred part, and directs it to the members rather than to the company.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 124(3) · Computing the twelve-per-cent interest
questions.stem: Kalindi Papers Limited was required to transfer ₹15,00,000 of unclaimed dividend to its Unpaid Dividend Account by 20 September 2026. It in fact made the transfer on 13 February 2027. The interest payable under section 124(3), taking a year of 365 days, is:

readLink.label: Read: Unpaid dividend and the Unpaid Dividend Account — section 124 →

options.explanation: That applies eighteen per cent. Eighteen per cent is the s. 127 rate for failing to pay dividend within thirty days; s. 124(3) fixes twelve per cent.
Correct. The default runs 146 days from 20 September 2026 to 13 February 2027, so ₹15,00,000 × 12/100 × 146/365 = ₹72,000, which enures to the benefit of the members.
That is twelve per cent for a full year. The interest runs only for the period of the default.
That is half the correct figure, produced by taking 73 days instead of 146.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · ss. 124(5) and 124(6) · The seven-year transfer
questions.stem: Money lying in a company's Unpaid Dividend Account, and the shares in respect of which dividend has remained unclaimed, are dealt with as follows:

readLink.label: Read: Unpaid dividend and the Unpaid Dividend Account — section 124 →

options.text: the money is transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund after seven years, but the shares remain with the shareholder in all cases
options.explanation: Section 124(6) requires the shares themselves to be transferred to the IEPF where dividend has been unpaid or unclaimed for seven consecutive years or more.

options.text: both the money and the shares are forfeited to the company after seven years
options.explanation: Nothing is forfeited to the company. The destination is the Fund, and the owner keeps a right to claim back.

options.text: the money, with any interest accrued, is transferred to the Fund after seven years from the date of its transfer to the Unpaid Dividend Account, and shares whose dividend has been unclaimed for seven consecutive years or more are transferred in the name of the Fund, the claimant retaining a right to claim the shares back
options.explanation: Correct. Section 124(5) moves the money with interest, s. 124(6) moves the shares, and the proviso to s. 124(6) preserves the claimant's right to claim a transfer of the shares from the IEPF.

options.text: the money is transferred to the Consolidated Fund of India and the shares are cancelled
options.explanation: Neither happens. The Investor Education and Protection Fund is the destination for the money, and the shares are transferred, not cancelled.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 125(3) · Utilisation of the IEPF
questions.stem: Which of the following is a purpose for which the Investor Education and Protection Fund may be utilised under section 125(3)?

readLink.label: Read: The Investor Education and Protection Fund — section 125 →

options.text: Reimbursement of legal expenses incurred in pursuing class action suits under sections 37 and 245 by members, debenture-holders or depositors, as sanctioned by the Tribunal
options.explanation: Correct. This is one of the enumerated uses, alongside refunds, investor education and awareness, and distribution of disgorged amounts under Court orders.

options.text: Payment of dividend to shareholders of loss-making companies that are unable to declare a dividend of their own
options.explanation: The Fund is not a substitute source of dividend. Section 123 alone governs where dividend may come from.

options.text: Meeting the administrative expenses of the Registrar of Companies
options.explanation: The Fund exists for investors, not for the administration of the registry.

options.text: Subscribing to the shares of small companies to improve their capital base
options.explanation: The Fund makes no equity investments in companies for that purpose; its uses are refunds, investor protection and the Court- and Tribunal-sanctioned payments the section names.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 126 · Dividend held in abeyance
questions.stem: An instrument of transfer of shares has been delivered to Lavanya Cables Limited for registration but the transfer has not yet been registered. As to the dividend and the rights and bonus entitlements on those shares, the company must:

readLink.label: Read: Dividend in abeyance — section 126 →

options.text: pay the dividend to the transferee named in the instrument and keep the rights and bonus entitlements in abeyance
options.explanation: The transferee may be paid only where the REGISTERED HOLDER has authorised it in writing. Absent that authority the dividend goes into the Unpaid Dividend Account.

options.text: pay the dividend to the registered holder and allot the rights and bonus shares to him as well
options.explanation: Section 126(b) requires the rights offer and the bonus issue to be kept in abeyance, not allotted to the transferor.

options.text: keep both the dividend and the rights and bonus entitlements in abeyance until the transfer is registered
options.explanation: Only the rights and bonus entitlements are kept in abeyance. The dividend has a specific destination — the Unpaid Dividend Account.

options.text: transfer the dividend to the Unpaid Dividend Account unless the registered holder has authorised in writing that it be paid to the transferee, and keep the rights offer under section 62(1)(a) and any fully paid bonus issue in abeyance
options.explanation: Correct. Section 126 splits the treatment exactly this way: the dividend is parked in the Unpaid Dividend Account subject to a written authority from the registered holder, while rights and bonus entitlements are frozen.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 127 · Computing the eighteen-per-cent interest
questions.stem: Saraswati Prints Limited declares a dividend on 10 July 2026. A sum of ₹36,50,000 is neither paid nor is the warrant posted, and the company finally pays it on 21 October 2026. Taking a year of 365 days and running the default from the expiry of the period allowed for payment, the simple interest payable by the company under section 127 is:

readLink.label: Read: Failure to pay — section 127 and its five defences →

options.explanation: That applies twelve per cent. Twelve per cent is the s. 124(3) rate for failing to transfer to the Unpaid Dividend Account; s. 127 fixes eighteen per cent.
Correct. Thirty days from 10 July 2026 expire on 9 August 2026, and 9 August to 21 October 2026 is 73 days. ₹36,50,000 × 18/100 × 73/365 = ₹1,31,400.
That is eighteen per cent for a full year. Interest runs only for the period during which the default continues.
That runs the interest for 103 days, from the date of declaration. The thirty days allowed for payment are not a period of default.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 127 · Consequences of failure to pay
questions.stem: Where a declared dividend is not paid and the warrant is not posted within thirty days of declaration, section 127 provides for:

readLink.label: Read: Failure to pay — section 127 and its five defences →

options.text: imprisonment of up to two years for every director of the company, and simple interest at twelve per cent per annum payable by the company
options.explanation: Two errors: only a director KNOWINGLY a party to the default is punishable, and the company's rate is eighteen per cent.

options.text: a penalty on the company of ₹1,000 for every day of default, and no other consequence
options.explanation: The ₹1,000 per day is part of the FINE on the knowingly-party director, and the company separately bears eighteen per cent interest.

options.text: imprisonment of up to two years together with a fine of not less than ₹1,000 for every day of continuing default, for every director knowingly a party to the default, and simple interest at eighteen per cent per annum payable by the company for the period of the default
options.explanation: Correct. Section 127 has these two distinct limbs — the director's punishment, which requires knowledge, and the company's interest, which does not.

options.text: compulsory transfer of the unpaid amount to the Investor Education and Protection Fund forthwith
options.explanation: The Fund receives the money only after seven years in the Unpaid Dividend Account. Section 127 is about punishment and interest.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 127 proviso · The five defences
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the circumstances in which the proviso to section 127 deems no offence to have been committed?

readLink.label: Read: Failure to pay — section 127 and its five defences →

options.text: Where the company had insufficient liquid funds to pay the dividend on the due date, although its profits were adequate
options.explanation: Correct as the answer to a NOT question. A shortage of cash is not a listed defence, and it is not a reason "not due to any default on the part of the company" — the company chose to declare a dividend it could not fund.

options.text: Where the dividend could not be paid by reason of the operation of any law
options.explanation: This is the first listed defence.

options.text: Where there is a dispute regarding the right to receive the dividend
options.explanation: This is the third listed defence, and it dovetails with s. 126, under which contested dividend is parked in the Unpaid Dividend Account.

options.text: Where the dividend has been lawfully adjusted by the company against a sum due to it from the shareholder
options.explanation: This is the fourth listed defence, and the word "lawfully" is load-bearing.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 51 · Dividend on the amount paid-up
questions.stem: Prakriti Foods Limited, whose articles authorise payment of dividend in proportion to the amount paid-up, declares a dividend of 12 per cent. Bhavna holds 20,000 equity shares of ₹10 each on which ₹7 per share has been paid up. Her dividend is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 51 read with Table F, Regulation 88

readLink.label: Read: Dividend in proportion to paid-up capital — section 51 →

options.explanation: That applies the rate to the nominal value of ₹2,00,000. That is the position only where the articles do NOT authorise proportional payment; here they do.
That applies 10 per cent to the paid-up amount of ₹1,40,000 instead of the declared 12 per cent.
That applies 12 per cent to ₹70,000, halving the holding to 10,000 shares.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 51 · Calls in advance
questions.stem: A member has paid to the company, in advance of calls, an amount not yet called up on his shares. For the purposes of dividend, that amount:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 51 read with s. 50(2)

readLink.label: Read: Dividend in proportion to paid-up capital — section 51 →

options.text: ranks equally with paid-up capital and carries dividend at the declared rate
options.explanation: Calls in advance are a debt owed by the company to the member, not paid-up capital, and they do not rank for dividend.

options.text: carries dividend at half the declared rate, the balance being paid as interest
options.explanation: There is no half-rate rule anywhere in the Act or in Table F.

options.text: is excluded from the base on which dividend is computed, though the articles may allow interest on it, and it carries no voting rights until it becomes presently payable
options.explanation: Correct. The s. 51 base is the amount called up and paid; the advance is a debt, typically remunerated by interest under the articles, and s. 50(2) denies voting rights on it until the money becomes presently payable.

options.text: is treated as paid-up capital only for a company that has adopted Table F
options.explanation: Adopting Table F changes nothing here. Regulation 88 measures dividend by amounts paid or credited as paid on the shares, which does not include an advance against uncalled capital.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · Revocation of a declared dividend
questions.stem: Three weeks after the members declared a final dividend at the annual general meeting, the Board discovers a large unforeseen liability and passes a resolution revoking the dividend. The revocation is:

readLink.label: Read: Revocation, and the master timeline →

options.text: effective, because the Board is entitled to reconsider a distribution in the interest of the company's solvency
options.explanation: Solvency concerns do not undo a debt that has already accrued to the shareholders.

options.text: ineffective, because a declared dividend becomes a debt due from the company to each shareholder and cannot be revoked, save where the declaration was itself unlawful or all the shareholders consent
options.explanation: Correct. Declaration creates an enforceable debt. Only an unlawful declaration, or the consent of all the shareholders, can undo it — and a Board resolution certainly cannot undo what the members declared.

options.text: effective if made before the expiry of the thirty days allowed for payment
options.explanation: The thirty-day period is the time allowed to discharge the debt, not a window in which the debt may be cancelled.

options.text: ineffective for a final dividend, but the same Board could lawfully revoke an interim dividend it had itself declared
options.explanation: Under the Companies Act 2013 an interim dividend stands on the same footing: s. 2(35) brings it within "dividend", s. 123(4) requires the same deposit and s. 127 applies the same clock and interest.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 123(1) · Sources out of which dividend may be declared
questions.stem: State the sources out of which a company may declare and pay dividend for a financial year under section 123(1) of the Companies Act 2013, and explain the restrictions contained in the provisos to that sub-section and in section 123(6). (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 123(1)(a): dividend may be declared out of the profits of the company for that financial year arrived at after providing for depreciation in accordance with section 123(2), or out of the profits of any previous financial year or years arrived at after providing for depreciation and remaining undistributed, or out of both; depreciation is to be provided in accordance with Schedule II
Section 123(1)(b): dividend may also be declared out of money provided by the Central Government or a State Government for the payment of dividend in pursuance of a guarantee given by that Government

First proviso: before declaring dividend a company MAY transfer such percentage of its profits for that year as it considers appropriate to its reserves; the transfer is voluntary, the compulsory slab of the 1956 Act having been discontinued

Third proviso: no dividend may be declared unless carried-over previous losses and depreciation not provided in previous year or years are set off against the profit of the company for the current year

Fourth proviso: no dividend may be declared or paid from reserves other than free reserves; and free reserves under section 2(43) exclude unrealised gains, notional gains, amounts representing revaluation of assets, and changes in the carrying amount of an asset or liability recognised in equity on fair-value measurement
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 123(1) fourth proviso, read with s. 2(43)

skeleton.point: Section 123(6): a company which fails to comply with sections 73 and 74 shall not, so long as such failure continues, declare any dividend on its equity shares; the bar is automatic and lifts when the default is cured

questions.topic: Ch 8 · Rule 3 · Dividend out of accumulated profits
questions.stem: Explain the conditions subject to which a company may declare dividend out of the accumulated profits earned in previous years and transferred to its free reserves, where its profits for the current year are inadequate or absent. Illustrate how the conditions interact where a company has a paid-up share capital of ₹9,00,00,000, free reserves of ₹5,00,00,000, a current-year loss of ₹40,00,000, and declared dividend at 14, 11 and 8 per cent in the three immediately preceding years. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: When the rules apply: the second proviso to section 123(1) requires that where, owing to inadequacy or absence of profits in any financial year, a company proposes to declare dividend out of accumulated profits earned in previous years and transferred to the free reserves, the declaration be made only in accordance with the prescribed rules, namely Rule 3 of the Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014

First condition: the rate of dividend declared shall not exceed the average of the rates at which dividend was declared in the three years immediately preceding that year; the condition does not apply to a company which has not declared any dividend in each of those three preceding financial years. On the figures, the average of 14, 11 and 8 is 11 per cent, so the dividend may not exceed 11% of ₹9,00,00,000 = ₹99,00,000
skeleton.citation: Rule 3(1) and its proviso, Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014

skeleton.point: Second condition: the total amount to be drawn from the accumulated profits shall not exceed one-tenth of the sum of the paid-up share capital and free reserves as appearing in the latest audited financial statement. On the figures, one-tenth of (₹9,00,00,000 + ₹5,00,00,000) = ₹1,40,00,000
skeleton.citation: Rule 3(2), Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014

skeleton.point: Third condition: the amount so drawn shall first be utilised to set off the losses incurred in the financial year in which the dividend is declared, before any dividend in respect of equity shares is declared. On the figures, ₹40,00,000 of the draw is absorbed by the current-year loss
skeleton.citation: Rule 3(3), Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014

skeleton.point: Fourth condition: the balance of reserves after such withdrawal shall not fall below fifteen per cent of the paid-up share capital as appearing in the latest audited financial statement. On the figures the floor is 15% of ₹9,00,00,000 = ₹1,35,00,000, so the draw may not exceed ₹5,00,00,000 − ₹1,35,00,000 = ₹3,65,00,000
skeleton.citation: Rule 3(4), Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014

skeleton.point: Conclusion on the interaction: every condition must be satisfied and the lowest ceiling governs. The binding draw ceiling is ₹1,40,00,000; after the ₹40,00,000 set-off, ₹1,00,00,000 remains, but the rate ceiling independently limits the dividend to ₹99,00,000. Maximum dividend = ₹99,00,000, total draw ₹1,39,00,000, reserves left ₹3,61,00,000, above the ₹1,35,00,000 floor
skeleton.citation: Rule 3, Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014 — application

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 123(3) · Interim dividend
questions.stem: Who may declare an interim dividend, during what period, and out of what sources? State also the restriction that applies where the company has incurred a loss during the current financial year. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Authority: the Board of Directors declares an interim dividend under section 123(3); no general meeting is involved. Section 2(35) provides that dividend includes any interim dividend, so every obligation attaching to dividend — deposit, payment and punishment — applies to it
Period: an interim dividend may be declared during any financial year, and also at any time during the period from the closure of the financial year till the holding of the annual general meeting

Sources: the surplus in the profit and loss account; or the profits of the financial year for which the interim dividend is sought to be declared; or the profits generated in the financial year till the quarter preceding the date of declaration of the interim dividend

Restriction on loss: where the company has incurred a loss during the current financial year up to the end of the quarter immediately preceding the date of declaration, the interim dividend shall not be declared at a rate higher than the average dividends declared by the company during the immediately preceding three financial years; the restriction limits the rate only, and does not import the one-tenth draw ceiling or the fifteen per cent reserve floor of Rule 3

Consequential obligations: the amount of the interim dividend must equally be deposited in a separate account with a scheduled bank within five days of declaration, and once declared an interim dividend is not revocable

questions.topic: Ch 8 · ss. 124 and 125 · Unpaid dividend and the IEPF
questions.stem: Trace what a company must do with a declared dividend that is not paid or claimed, from the expiry of the period allowed for payment until the money and the shares reach the Investor Education and Protection Fund, and state what remedy the shareholder retains at each stage. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Where a dividend declared has not been paid or claimed within thirty days from the date of declaration, the company shall, within seven days from the date of expiry of that period of thirty days, transfer the total unpaid or unclaimed amount to a special account opened in any scheduled bank called the Unpaid Dividend Account

Within ninety days of making any such transfer the company shall prepare a statement containing the names, last known addresses and the unpaid dividend payable to each person, and place it on its own website, if any, and on any other website approved by the Central Government

On default in transferring the whole or any part of the amount, the company shall pay interest at twelve per cent per annum from the date of the default on the amount not transferred, and that interest enures to the benefit of the members in proportion to the amounts remaining unpaid to them
Remedy at the first stage: any person claiming to be entitled to money transferred to the Unpaid Dividend Account may apply to the COMPANY for payment

Money remaining unpaid or unclaimed for seven years from the date of transfer to the Unpaid Dividend Account is transferred, with any interest accrued, to the Fund established under section 125(1); the company sends a statement of the details to the administering authority, which issues a receipt as evidence of the transfer

All shares in respect of which dividend has not been paid or claimed for seven consecutive years or more are transferred in the name of the Investor Education and Protection Fund with a statement in the prescribed form; the claimant is entitled to claim the transfer of those shares back from the Fund, and a person whose amount has been transferred may apply to the Authority for refund
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 124(6) and its proviso, read with s. 125(4)

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 127 · Punishment for failure to distribute dividend
questions.stem: State the circumstances in which section 127 of the Companies Act 2013 is attracted, the consequences for the company and for its directors, and the circumstances in which no offence is deemed to have been committed. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Trigger: a dividend has been declared by the company but has not been paid, or the warrant in respect of it has not been posted, within thirty days from the date of declaration, to any shareholder entitled to payment; by virtue of section 2(35) this applies to an interim dividend as well
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 127 read with s. 2(35)

skeleton.point: Liability of directors: every director of the company who is KNOWINGLY a party to the default is punishable with imprisonment which may extend to two years and with fine which shall not be less than ₹1,000 for every day during which the default continues

Liability of the company: the company is liable to pay simple interest at the rate of eighteen per cent per annum during the period for which the default continues; the liability is automatic and does not depend on knowledge or on any order

The five statutory defences under the proviso: (a) where the dividend could not be paid by reason of the operation of any law; (b) where a shareholder has given directions regarding payment which cannot be complied with and the same has been communicated to him; (c) where there is a dispute regarding the right to receive the dividend; (d) where the dividend has been lawfully adjusted by the company against any sum due to it from the shareholder; and (e) where for any other reason the failure to pay or to post the warrant was not due to any default on the part of the company

Distinguish section 124(3): the twelve per cent per annum there is charged for failure to TRANSFER unpaid dividend to the Unpaid Dividend Account and enures to the members, whereas the eighteen per cent under section 127 is charged for failure to PAY within thirty days
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 124(3) contrasted with s. 127

questions.topic: Ch 8 · s. 51 · Proportional dividend, calls in advance and revocation
questions.stem: Explain the rule in section 51 of the Companies Act 2013 relating to payment of dividend in proportion to the amount paid-up, the treatment of calls paid in advance, and whether a dividend once declared may be revoked. (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 51: a company MAY, IF SO AUTHORISED BY ITS ARTICLES, pay dividends in proportion to the amount paid-up on each share; the power is permissive and is conditional on an enabling provision in the articles

Position where the articles do not so authorise: dividend follows the nominal amount of the shares, so a partly paid share of a given denomination carries the same dividend as a fully paid share of that denomination
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 51 — converse of the enabling condition

skeleton.point: Table F: Regulation 88 of Table F in Schedule I contains the enabling provision, so a company that has adopted Table F already has the power and need not amend its articles
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, Table F, Schedule I, Regulation 88

skeleton.point: Calls in advance: money paid in advance of calls is a debt owed by the company to the member and is not paid-up capital; it is excluded from the base on which dividend is computed, the articles usually providing for interest on it instead, and it carries no voting rights until it becomes presently payable
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 51 read with s. 50(2)

skeleton.point: Revocation: a dividend once declared becomes a debt due from the company to each shareholder and cannot be revoked, save where the declaration was itself unlawful or all the shareholders consent; under the 2013 Act an interim dividend stands on the same footing, section 2(35) bringing it within dividend and sections 123(4) and 127 applying to it

questions.topic: Ch 8 · Case: declaring dividend out of accumulated profits
questions.case: Mrinalini Instruments Limited closes its financial year on 31 March 2026 with a profit of only ₹18,00,000 after providing depreciation in accordance with Schedule II — far short of what the Board wishes to distribute. Its latest audited financial statement shows a paid-up equity share capital of ₹12,00,00,000 and free reserves of ₹7,00,00,000, built up from the undistributed profits of earlier years. The company declared dividend at 15 per cent, 12 per cent and 9 per cent in the three financial years immediately preceding. It has no carried-over losses, no unprovided depreciation and no default under sections 73 or 74. The Board resolves to recommend the largest dividend the law permits, drawing the shortfall from the accumulated profits standing in the free reserves.

readLink.label: Read: Dividend out of accumulated profits — Rule 3 →

questions.stem: The proposal to draw on the accumulated profits is governed by:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 123(1), second proviso, read with Rule 3

options.text: section 123(1)(b), the accumulated profits being treated as money provided for the payment of dividend
options.explanation: Section 123(1)(b) concerns money provided by the Central or a State Government under a government guarantee. It has nothing to do with a company's own reserves.

options.text: the second proviso to section 123(1) read with Rule 3 of the Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014, because the profits for the year are inadequate
options.explanation: Correct. The second proviso engages on inadequacy or absence of profits and sends the declaration to the prescribed rules, which are the three ceilings and the set-off in Rule 3.

options.text: section 123(1)(a), the reserves being undistributed profits of previous financial years, so that no further conditions apply
options.explanation: Undistributed earlier-year profits are indeed a source under s. 123(1)(a), but where the current year's profits are inadequate and the company draws on accumulated profits transferred to free reserves, the second proviso superimposes Rule 3.

options.text: section 63, since a distribution out of accumulated profits is in substance a capitalisation of reserves
options.explanation: Section 63 governs bonus shares, which are a capitalisation. This is a cash dividend and no capitalisation occurs.

questions.stem: The maximum total amount that Mrinalini Instruments Limited may draw from its accumulated profits is:
questions.sourceRef: Rule 3(2), Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014

options.explanation: That is one-tenth of the paid-up share capital alone. The second condition is measured on the SUM of paid-up share capital and free reserves.
That is one-tenth of the free reserves alone, dropping the paid-up capital from the base.
Correct. One-tenth of (₹12,00,00,000 + ₹7,00,00,000) = one-tenth of ₹19,00,00,000 = ₹1,90,00,000. The fifteen-per-cent floor permits a much larger draw here, so the one-tenth ceiling governs.
That is the headroom to the fifteen-per-cent floor: ₹7,00,00,000 less 15% of ₹12,00,00,000. It is a ceiling too, but the lower one-tenth ceiling governs.

questions.stem: The maximum dividend Mrinalini Instruments Limited may declare for the year, taking all the conditions together, is:
questions.sourceRef: Rule 3(1) and 3(2), Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014

options.explanation: Correct. The rate ceiling is the average of 15, 12 and 9 = 12 per cent, so 12% × ₹12,00,00,000 = ₹1,44,00,000. Of that, ₹18,00,000 comes from the year's profit and ₹1,26,00,000 from the reserves, within the ₹1,90,00,000 draw ceiling.
That is the draw ceiling, not the dividend ceiling. The rate condition independently caps the dividend at 12 per cent of the paid-up capital.
That is fifteen per cent of the paid-up share capital — the base of the reserve floor, which prescribes what must be LEFT, and it is not a rate of dividend.
That adds the full draw ceiling of ₹1,90,00,000 to the current year's profit of ₹18,00,000, ignoring the rate ceiling altogether.

questions.stem: Suppose instead that Mrinalini Instruments Limited had declared no dividend at all in each of the three immediately preceding financial years. The effect on the Rule 3 analysis would be that:
questions.sourceRef: Proviso to Rule 3(1), Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules 2014

options.text: Rule 3 would cease to apply altogether and the company could distribute the whole of its free reserves
options.explanation: Only the rate condition is lifted. The draw ceiling and the reserve floor continue to apply, and the fourth proviso to s. 123(1) still confines the source to free reserves.

options.text: the rate would be capped at nil, there being no average to work from
options.explanation: The proviso is a relaxation, not a prohibition. It exists precisely because a nil average would otherwise block any dividend.

options.text: the one-tenth draw ceiling would be lifted but the rate ceiling would continue at nil
options.explanation: This inverts the proviso. It relieves against the rate condition, not against the draw condition.

options.text: the rate ceiling in the first condition would not apply, while the one-tenth draw ceiling, the fifteen-per-cent reserve floor and the set-off of current-year losses would continue to apply
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso to Rule 3(1) disapplies only the rate condition for a company that declared no dividend in each of the three preceding years; the remaining conditions are untouched.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · Case: the declaration-to-IEPF timeline
questions.case: At its annual general meeting held on 24 August 2026, Haritha Agro Limited declares a final dividend of ₹1,80,00,000 on the recommendation of its Board. The company pays the great majority of it on time, but ₹9,00,000 remains neither paid nor claimed when the period allowed for payment expires, most of it belonging to members whose addresses on the register are out of date. A further ₹1,20,000 relates to shares for which an instrument of transfer was lodged with the company on 2 August 2026 and which has not yet been registered; the registered holder has given no written authority to pay the transferee.

readLink.label: Read: Revocation, and the master timeline →

questions.stem: Within five days of 24 August 2026 the company must deposit the amount of the dividend:

options.text: in the Unpaid Dividend Account opened under section 124
options.explanation: The Unpaid Dividend Account receives only what remains unpaid or unclaimed at the end of the thirty-day period. It is a later account with a different purpose.

options.text: in the company's ordinary current account, provided the amount is disclosed as dividend payable in the notes to the accounts
options.explanation: Section 123(4) requires physical segregation in a SEPARATE account, not a disclosure in the accounts.

options.text: in a separate account opened for the purpose with a scheduled bank
options.explanation: Correct. Section 123(4) requires the amount of the dividend, including interim dividend, to be deposited in a separate account with a scheduled bank within five days of declaration.

options.text: with the Investor Education and Protection Fund Authority, pending payment to the shareholders
options.explanation: The Fund is reached only after seven years in the Unpaid Dividend Account, and never as a first destination.

questions.stem: The last date by which the unpaid ₹9,00,000 must be transferred to the Unpaid Dividend Account is:

options.text: 31 August 2026
options.explanation: That counts the seven days from the date of declaration. Section 124(1) counts them from the expiry of the thirty-day payment period.

options.text: 30 September 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Thirty days from 24 August 2026 expire on 23 September 2026, and seven days from that expiry gives 30 September 2026.

options.text: 23 September 2026
options.explanation: That is the expiry of the thirty-day payment period itself. The seven-day transfer period begins there.

options.text: 29 August 2026
options.explanation: That is the five-day deposit deadline under s. 123(4), a different obligation running from the same declaration date.

questions.stem: As to the ₹1,20,000 relating to the shares whose transfer has been lodged but not registered, the company must:

options.text: pay it to the transferee named in the instrument of transfer, the company having notice of his interest
options.explanation: Notice of the transfer is not enough. Payment to the transferee needs the written authority of the registered holder, which has not been given.

options.text: pay it to the registered holder, who remains the member on the register until the transfer is registered
options.explanation: Section 126(a) removes that option. The dividend goes into the Unpaid Dividend Account instead, unless the registered holder authorises payment to the transferee in writing.

options.text: retain it in the separate account opened under section 123(4) until the transfer is registered
options.explanation: Section 126 specifies the destination, and it is the Unpaid Dividend Account under s. 124, not the s. 123(4) deposit account.

options.text: transfer it to the Unpaid Dividend Account, and in addition keep in abeyance any rights offer under section 62(1)(a) and any fully paid bonus issue in relation to those shares
options.explanation: Correct. Section 126 sends the dividend to the Unpaid Dividend Account in the absence of a written authority from the registered holder, and freezes rights and bonus entitlements until the register is settled.

questions.stem: Assume the transfer to the Unpaid Dividend Account is made on 30 September 2026 and part of the money is never claimed. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A statement of the names, last known addresses and amounts must be placed on the company's website, if any, and on any approved website within ninety days of 30 September 2026; and money still unclaimed on 30 September 2033 must go to the Fund with any interest accrued, along with the shares concerned, the claimant retaining the right to apply to the Authority
options.explanation: Correct. The ninety days under s. 124(2) run from the date of the transfer, the seven years under s. 124(5) run from the same date, s. 124(6) carries the shares across, and ss. 124(6) and 125(4) preserve the claim.

options.text: The ninety-day statement and the seven-year transfer both run from 24 August 2026, the date of declaration
options.explanation: Both clocks run from the date of the transfer into the Unpaid Dividend Account, not from the declaration. This is the most common date error in the chapter.

options.text: Money still unclaimed after seven years is written back to the profit and loss account of the company
options.explanation: Writing back is precisely what s. 124(5) prevents. The money goes to the Investor Education and Protection Fund.

options.text: The shares remain with the shareholders whatever happens, only the money being transferred to the Fund
options.explanation: Section 124(6) requires shares whose dividend has been unpaid or unclaimed for seven consecutive years or more to be transferred in the name of the Fund.

questions.topic: Ch 8 · Case: failure to pay a declared dividend
questions.case: Tungabhadra Paints Limited declares a dividend on 10 July 2026. A block of ₹50,00,000 payable to one institutional shareholder is neither paid nor is any warrant posted, because the finance director decided to use the money for a working-capital shortfall; the company finally pays the shareholder on 21 October 2026. Director K was fully aware of the decision and concurred in it. Separately, ₹4,00,000 payable to another member could not be paid because two rival claimants are before a civil court disputing which of them is entitled to receive it.

readLink.label: Read: Failure to pay — section 127 and its five defences →

questions.stem: As regards the ₹50,00,000, the position of Director K and of the company under section 127 is that:

options.text: neither is liable, since the shareholder has ultimately been paid in full
options.explanation: Late payment does not undo the default. Section 127 is attracted by the failure to pay or post the warrant within thirty days.

options.text: the company alone is liable, a director being liable only where the Tribunal so orders
options.explanation: No order of the Tribunal is needed. A director knowingly a party to the default is punishable under the section itself.

options.text: Director K is liable to a penalty of ₹1,000 per day and the company to interest at twelve per cent per annum
options.explanation: The rate is wrong — s. 127 fixes eighteen per cent for the company — and the director's ₹1,000 per day is a minimum FINE accompanying imprisonment, not a stand-alone penalty.

options.text: Director K, being knowingly a party to the default, is punishable with imprisonment which may extend to two years and with a fine of not less than ₹1,000 for every day the default continues, and the company is liable to pay simple interest at eighteen per cent per annum for the period of the default
options.explanation: Correct. Section 127 has two independent limbs, and K's knowledge and concurrence satisfy the "knowingly a party" requirement.

questions.stem: As regards the ₹4,00,000 caught up in the dispute between rival claimants, the company:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, proviso to s. 127, read with s. 126

options.text: is liable to eighteen per cent interest on that amount as well, the dispute being no concern of the company
options.explanation: The proviso deems no offence to have been committed where there is a dispute regarding the right to receive the dividend, so neither limb of s. 127 follows.

options.text: must pay the amount to whichever claimant applies first, and recover it later if the court decides otherwise
options.explanation: Paying a claimant whose entitlement is disputed is exactly what the statutory scheme avoids. The money is parked instead.

options.text: commits no offence, because there is a dispute regarding the right to receive the dividend; the money is meanwhile held for whoever is found entitled
options.explanation: Correct. Defence (c) in the proviso to s. 127 applies squarely, so no offence is deemed committed and no eighteen per cent interest runs on that amount.

options.text: must transfer the amount immediately to the Investor Education and Protection Fund pending the court's decision
options.explanation: The Fund is reached only after seven years in the Unpaid Dividend Account. An immediate transfer to the Fund is never right.

questions.stem: Taking a year of 365 days and running the default from the expiry of the period allowed for payment, the simple interest the company must pay on the ₹50,00,000 is:

options.explanation: Correct. Thirty days from 10 July 2026 expire on 9 August 2026, and 9 August to 21 October 2026 is 73 days; ₹50,00,000 × 18/100 × 73/365 = ₹1,80,000.
That applies twelve per cent — the s. 124(3) rate for failing to transfer to the Unpaid Dividend Account, not the s. 127 rate.
That is eighteen per cent for a full year, ignoring that the default lasted 73 days.
That is eighteen per cent for half a year, which is roughly twice the actual period of default.
